statement: A real linear space V is said to have an inner product if to each pair of elements x, y there corresponds a unique real number (x, y) satisfying four axioms: symmetry, distributivity (linearity), homogeneity in the scalar, and positivity for nonzero x. Apostol defines the product axiomatically rather than by a specific formula.

statement: A linear space that is not finite dimensional is called infinite dimensional. The space of all polynomials is an example: an infinite set of powers of t spans it, but no finite set of polynomials does.

statement: Given a linear space V, a nonempty subset S of V is called a subspace of V if S is itself a linear space under the same operations of addition and multiplication by scalars.
quotes: If S is also a linear space, with the same operations of addition and multiplication by scalars, then S is called a subspace of V.
Given a linear space V, let S be a nonempty subset of V.

statement: In a Euclidean space V, two elements x and y are called orthogonal if their inner product is zero. The zero element is orthogonal to every element of V, and it is the only element orthogonal to itself.
quotes: DEFINITION. In a Euclidean space V, two elements x and y are called orthogonal if their inner product is zero.
The zero element is orthogonal to every element of V; it is the only element orthogonal to itself.

quotes: THEOREM 15.5. Let S be an independent set consisting of k elements in a linear space V
Then every set of $k + 1$ elements in $L(S)$ is dependent.

statement: A finite set S of elements in a linear space V is called a finite basis for V if S is independent and spans V.
quotes: DEFINITION. A finite set S of elements in a linear space V is called a finite basis for V if S is independent and spans V.

quotes: THEOREM 15.3. In a given linear space, let $x$ and $y$ denote arbitrary elements and let $a$ and $b$ denote arbitrary scalars. Then we have the following properties:

statement: L(S) denotes the subspace spanned by the set S, i.e. the set of all finite linear combinations of elements of S. It is used throughout, for instance in the statement of Theorem 15.5.
quotes: We call this the subspace spanned by S, or the linear span of S, and denote it by $L(S)$
and let $L(S)$ be the subspace spanned by S.

statement: The negative of x is denoted by -x, and the difference y - x is defined to be the sum y + (-x).
quotes: Notation. The negative of $x$ is denoted by $-x$ . The difference $y - x$ is defined to be the sum $y + (-x)$

statement: In any linear space there is one and only one zero element. The proof uses Axiom 5 for existence and the commutative law to show two candidates O_1 and O_2 must coincide.
quotes: THEOREM 15.1. UNIQUENESS OF THE ZERO ELEMENT. In any linear space there is one and only one zero element.

statement: A function space is a linear space whose elements are real-valued functions, with (f + g)(x) = f(x) + g(x), with af the function whose value at x is af(x), and with the everywhere-zero function as zero element.
quotes: The following examples are called function spaces. The elements of V are real-valued functions, with addition of two functions f and g defined in the usual way:
Multiplication of a function f by a real scalar a is defined as follows: af is that function whose value at each x in the domain of f is $af(x)$ .

statement: THEOREM 15.4: if S is a nonempty subset of a linear space V, then S is a subspace if and only if S satisfies the closure axioms. The proof shows the remaining axioms are inherited from V or follow from closure.
quotes: THEOREM 15.4. Let S be a nonempty subset of a linear space V. Then S is a subspace if and only if S satisfies the closure axioms.
If S is a subspace, it satisfies all the axioms for a linear space, and hence, in particular, it satisfies the closure axioms.
Now we show that if S satisfies the closure axioms it satisfies the others as well.

statement: A complex linear space with an inner product is called a complex Euclidean space; the term unitary space is also used. One example is the complex vector space V_n(C).
quotes: A complex linear space with an inner product is called a complex Euclidean space. (Sometimes the term unitary space is also used.)

statement: A linear space equipped with an inner product. When the term Euclidean space is used without further designation the space may be real or complex, and the theorems of the chapter hold in either case. The inner product is what introduces the metric concept of length into such a space.
quotes: When we use the term Euclidean space without further designation, it is to be understood that the space can be real or complex.
The inner product can be used to introduce the metric concept of length in any Euclidean space.

statement: The third group of axioms (Axioms 7 to 10): a(bx) = (ab)x, a(x + y) = ax + ay, (a + b)x = ax + bx, and 1x = x for every x in V and all real a and b.

AXIOM 7. ASSOCIATIVE LAW. For every x in V and all real numbers a and b, we have

quotes: EXAMPLE 7. If $a_1, \ldots, a_n$ are distinct real numbers, the $n$ exponential functions
are independent. We can prove this by induction on $n$ . The result holds trivially when $n = 1$ .

statement: The numbers used as multipliers of the elements of V are called scalars. A real linear space has real numbers as scalars, a complex linear space has complex numbers as scalars.
quotes: Sometimes a linear space is referred to as a linear vector space or simply a vector space; the numbers used as multipliers are also called scalars.
A real linear space has real numbers as scalars; a complex linear space has complex numbers as scalars.

statement: Part (d) of Theorem 15.9: ||x + y|| <= ||x|| + ||y|| for all elements x and y of a Euclidean space. The equality sign holds if x = O, if y = O, or if y = cx for some c > 0. The proof expands ||x + y||^2 and applies the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.

statement: In a Euclidean space V the norm of x is the nonnegative number ||x|| = (x, x)^(1/2). It is the metric notion of length in a Euclidean space, and since an inner product can be defined in many different ways, the norm of an element depends on the choice of inner product.

statement: The set of all finite linear combinations of elements of S satisfies the closure axioms and is therefore a subspace of V; it is called the subspace spanned by S, or the linear span of S. If S is empty the span is defined to be the set consisting of the zero element alone.
quotes: The set of all finite linear combinations of elements of S satisfies the closure axioms and hence is a subspace of V.
We call this the subspace spanned by S, or the linear span of S, and denote it by $L(S)$

statement: The dot product x . y of two vectors in V_n, defined in Chapter 12 by the sum of the products of corresponding components. It is the concrete product in terms of which lengths and angles in V_n were defined, and it is the model that the inner product generalizes; in V_n one may take (x, y) = x . y.
quotes: In our study of $V_{n}$ , we defined lengths and angles in terms of the dot product.
EXAMPLE 1. In $V_{n}$ let $(x, y) = x \cdot y$ , the usual dot product of $x$ and $y$ .

statement: A set spans a space when every element of the space is a finite linear combination of its elements. Different sets may span the same subspace, and Apostol asks which spaces can be spanned by a finite set and with how few elements.
quotes: Different sets may span the same subspace. For example, the space $V_{2}$ is spanned by each of the following sets of vectors
For example, which spaces can be spanned by a finite set of elements?
The space of all polynomials is spanned by the infinite set of polynomials

statement: A linear space is a nonempty set V of elements of any kind on which addition and multiplication by numbers can be performed, subject to ten axioms listed in three groups. The nature of the elements and of the operations is not specified; only the axioms are required.
quotes: Briefly, a linear space is a set of elements of any kind on which certain operations (called addition and multiplication by numbers) can be performed.
The set V is called a linear space if it satisfies the following ten axioms which we list in three groups.
In this chapter we discuss a general mathematical concept, called a linear space, which includes all these examples and many others as special cases.

statement: A subset S of a Euclidean space V is called an orthogonal set if (x, y) = 0 for every pair of distinct elements x and y in S. Example: the trigonometric system in C(0, 2pi) with the integral inner product is an orthogonal set.
quotes: A subset S of V is called an orthogonal set if $(x, y) = 0$ for every pair of distinct elements x and y in S.
so S is an orthogonal set. Since no member of S is the zero element, S is independent.

Apostol states these properties and regards them as axioms.
quotes: That is, we state a number of properties we wish inner products to satisfy and we regard these properties as axioms.

The term is also applied to the elements themselves, and unlike the Chapter 12 definition it is not restricted to finite sets.
quotes: The set $S$ is called independent if it is not dependent.
For example, the elements in an independent set are called independent elements.
However, the present definition is not restricted to finite sets.

statement: If a linear space V has a basis of n elements, the integer n is called the dimension of V. The space consisting of the zero element alone is said to have dimension 0.
quotes: DEFINITION. If a linear space V has a basis of n elements, the integer n is called the dimension of V.
If $V = \{O\}$ , we say V has dimension 0.

statement: In a complex linear space an inner product (x, y) is a complex number satisfying the same axioms as a real inner product, except that symmetry is replaced by (x, y) = conjugate of (y, x). The scalar multiplier in the homogeneity axiom may be any complex number, and the companion relation (x, cy) = conjugate(c) (x, y) follows.

statement: In a linear space of dimension n one may consider a basis whose elements e_1, ..., e_n are taken in a given order; such an ordered basis is denoted as the n-tuple (e_1, ..., e_n).
quotes: Let $V$ be a linear space of dimension $n$ and consider a basis whose elements $e_1, \ldots, e_n$ are taken in a given order.
We denote such an ordered basis as an $n$ -tuple $(e_1, \ldots, e_n)$

statement: A linear space V is called finite dimensional if it has a finite basis, or if V consists of the zero element O alone.
quotes: The space V is called finite dimensional if it has a finite basis, or if V consists of O alone.

statement: In a real Euclidean space V the angle between two nonzero elements x and y is the number theta in [0, pi] with cos theta = (x, y) / (||x|| ||y||). The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality shows the quotient lies in [-1, 1], so exactly one such theta exists.
quotes: DEFINITION. In a real Euclidean space V, the angle between two nonzero elements x and y is defined to be that number $\theta$ in the interval $0 \leq \theta \leq \pi$ which satisfies the equation
\cos \theta = \frac {(x , y)}{\| x \| \| y \|}.\tag{15.6}

statement: The set of all polynomials of degree equal to n is not a linear space, because the closure axioms are not satisfied: the sum of two polynomials of degree n need not have degree n.
quotes: The set of all polynomials of degree equal to n is not a linear space because the closure axioms are not satisfied.
For example, the sum of two polynomials of degree n need not have degree n.

statement: On C(a, b), the linear space of all real-valued functions continuous on [a, b], an inner product of f and g is defined by the integral of f(t)g(t) over [a, b]. The function values f(t) and g(t) play the role of the components, and integration takes the place of summation.
quotes: EXAMPLE 3. Let $C(a, b)$ denote the linear space of all real-valued functions continuous on an interval $[a, b]$ . Define an inner product of two functions $f$ and $g$ by the formula
The function values $f(t)$ and $g(t)$ play the role of the components $x_{i}$ and $y_{i}$ , and integration takes the place of summation.

statement: THEOREM 15.10: in a Euclidean space V, every orthogonal set of nonzero elements is independent. In particular, in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space with dim V = n, every orthogonal set consisting of n nonzero elements is a basis for V.
quotes: THEOREM 15.10. In a Euclidean space V, every orthogonal set of nonzero elements is independent.
In particular, in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space with dim V = n, every orthogonal set consisting of n nonzero elements is a basis for V.

This is logically equivalent to the statement that every subset of an independent set is independent.

statement: A linear space as defined by the ten axioms is sometimes called a real linear space, to emphasize that the elements of V are multiplied by real numbers. Its scalars are the real numbers.
quotes: Linear spaces, as defined above, are sometimes called real linear spaces to emphasize the fact that we are multiplying the elements of V by real numbers.

statement: THEOREM 15.6: if V is a finite-dimensional linear space, then every finite basis for V has the same number of elements. The proof compares two bases of k and m elements and uses Theorem 15.5 twice to get m <= k and k <= m.
quotes: Then every finite basis for $V$ has the same number of elements.
Let S and T be two finite bases for V. Suppose S consists of k elements and T consists of m elements.

statement: THEOREM 15.9: in a Euclidean space, every norm satisfies, for all x, y and all scalars c: (a) ||x|| = 0 if x = O; (b) ||x|| > 0 if x is not O (positivity); (c) ||cx|| = |c| ||x|| (homogeneity); (d) ||x + y|| <= ||x|| + ||y|| (triangle inequality). These properties do not depend on the choice of inner product.

statement: In a general linear space the inner product of x and y is written (x, y), in place of the dot product notation x . y used in V_n. Taking c = 0 in the homogeneity axiom gives (O, y) = 0 for all y.
quotes: In a general linear space, we write $(x, y)$ instead of $x \cdot y$ for inner products
Note: Taking $c = 0$ in (3), we find that $(O, y) = 0$ for all $y$ .

statement: If real number is replaced by complex number in Axioms 2, 7, 8 and 9, the resulting structure is a complex linear space; its scalars are the complex numbers. All the theorems proved for real linear spaces are valid for complex linear spaces as well.
quotes: If real number is replaced by complex number in Axioms 2, 7, 8, and 9, the resulting structure is called a complex linear space.
Although we shall deal primarily with examples of real linear spaces, all the theorems are valid for complex linear spaces as well.

statement: An orthogonal set is called orthonormal if each of its elements has norm 1. Dividing each element of an orthogonal set by its norm produces an orthonormal set.
quotes: An orthogonal set is called orthonormal if each of its elements has norm 1.
Dividing each $u_{n}$ by its norm, we obtain an orthonormal set $\{\varphi_0,\varphi_1,\varphi_2,\ldots \}$ where $\varphi_{n} = u_{n} / \| u_{n}\|$ .

statement: By Axiom 6, for every x in V the element (-1)x satisfies x + (-1)x = O, so each x has at least one negative, namely (-1)x.
quotes: AXIOM 6. EXISTENCE OF NEGATIVES. For every x in V, the element $(-1)x$ has the property
Axiom 6 tells us that each x has at least one negative, namely $(-1)x$

statement: Example 8: the set of all functions continuous on a given interval is a function space; when the interval is [a, b] this space is denoted by C(a, b).
quotes: EXAMPLE 8. The set of all functions continuous on a given interval. If the interval is $[a, b]$ , we denote this space by $C(a, b)$

statement: Example 12: the set of all solutions of the homogeneous equation y'' + ay' + by = 0, with a and b given constants, is a function space. The 0 on the right is essential; the solution set of a nonhomogeneous equation does not satisfy the closure axioms.
quotes: EXAMPLE 12. The set of all solutions of a homogeneous linear differential equation $y'' + ay' + by = 0$ , where a and b are given constants.
The set of solutions of a nonhomogeneous differential equation does not satisfy the closure axioms.

statement: In any linear space every element has exactly one negative: for every x there is one and only one y such that x + y = O, and that y is the element (-1)x.
quotes: THEOREM 15.2. UNIQUENESS OF NEGATIVE ELEMENTS. In any linear space every element has exactly one negative. That is, for every x there is one and only one y such that $x + y = O$
Therefore $y_{1} = y_{2}$ , so $x$ has exactly one negative, the element $(-1)x$ .

statement: A real linear space with an inner product is called a real Euclidean space. These are the examples Apostol is primarily interested in, and proofs given for V_n carry over verbatim to any real Euclidean space.
quotes: A real linear space with an inner product is called a real Euclidean space.
Therefore, the very same proof is valid in any real Euclidean space.

statement: The first group of axioms (Axioms 1 and 2): every pair x, y in V has a unique sum x + y in V, and every x in V together with every real number a has a product ax in V.
quotes: AXIOM 1. CLOSURE UNDER ADDITION. For every pair of elements x and y in V there corresponds a unique element in V called the sum of x and y
AXIOM 2. CLOSURE UNDER MULTIPLICATION BY REAL NUMBERS. For every x in V and every real number a there corresponds an element in V called the product of a and x, denoted by ax.

statement: Axiom 5 postulates an element of V, denoted by O, with x + O = x for all x in V. In a function space the zero element is the function whose values are everywhere zero.
quotes: AXIOM 5. EXISTENCE OF ZERO ELEMENT. There is an element in V, denoted by O, such that
Axiom 5 tells us that there is at least one zero element.

statement: The coefficients in the expansion x = sum c_i e_i over a basis determine an n-tuple (c_1, ..., c_n) that is uniquely determined by x: subtracting a second representation and using independence of the basis elements gives c_i = d_i for each i.
quotes: The coefficients in this equation determine an n-tuple of numbers $(c_{1},\ldots,c_{n})$ that is uniquely determined by x.
